MACHINE TRAP, cost three attempts on 2026-09-07: the Bash tool's heredoc collapses a doubled backslash even when the delimiter is QUOTED. `python - <<'PY'` should pass its body verbatim, and does not: a Python string written as "a\runs" arrives as "auns", so  becomes a carriage return and c raises an invalid-escape SyntaxWarning. It corrupted a documented path into `...windowsweep<CR>uns<id>` and, worse, silently broke a plant script into a SyntaxError - after which the test it was meant to make fail reported "ok", which reads exactly like a passing gate. The three habits that work: build every backslash from `chr(92)` or `String.fromCharCode(92)` and concatenate; or write the file with a python raw string `r\"\"\"...\"\"\"`; or read the real source off disk and operate on it instead of retyping it. And always print the changed line back as proof a plant applied - a no-op edit is indistinguishable from a gate that failed to fire.

Every layout check, every word check and every contrast measurement passed it: the text was correct, the layout was correct, and the figure was zero. The `1 sections` was the only tell. Cause: the hero and the rail read a RUN's result off a SCAN's summary, because `--scan` populates targets[] and leaves estimated_bytes at 0 while sections[] holds only the steps that ran. Fixed and PROVED on the running app 2026-09-07: hero 59.3 GB, `across 665 targets in 10 sections`, button `Reclaim 59.3 GB`, rail `59.3 GB across 10 sections`, ladder still 39.3 GB. 🔴 The 59.3-beside-39.3 difference is BY DESIGN (wire.js:436-442 - hero and button show the total, the ladder shows the safe-batch subset) and must not be 'fixed' by a later reader; it is written into lib/reclaim.ts's header for exactly that reason.

🔴 THE SAME FIGURE WAS COMPUTED IN TWO FILES AND WAS WRONG THE SAME WAY IN BOTH - Home.tsx and Shell.tsx each derived the reclaimable bytes independently. Duplication did not merely risk drift; it doubled one defect and made the screen contradict itself in two places at once. It now lives once in lib/reclaim.ts, along with the map-target mapping that Home and Run both need. The generalisable form of the single-home rule: a DERIVED figure shown on more than one surface gets one home, or the surfaces will eventually disagree - and when they do, the reader believes the one that looks most official.

MACHINE TRAP, hit twice more on 2026-09-07 with two different shapes. (1) A regex written into a probe through a heredoc collapsed its escape, so `.replace(/\s+/g,' ')` became `.replace(/s+/g,' ')` and STRIPPED EVERY LETTER S from the output - it read 'not mea ured' and 'Dry-run fir t'. Build every regex from String.fromCharCode(92). (2) 🔴 A structure check compared innerText CASE-SENSITIVELY and reported two present structures as missing: `.caps` applies text-transform: uppercase and innerText reflects the RENDERED text, so 'What is going' reads back as 'WHAT IS GOING'. Compare case-insensitively, or against the rendered form. Both produced confident wrong answers about a working build, which is the expensive direction.

BASELINE FOR THE RELEASE, measured 2026-09-07 before any desktop release exists: the updater endpoint https://github.com/aoneahsan/windowsweep/releases/latest/download/latest.json returns 404. That is expected and is the concrete case IRON rule 13 exists to prevent permanently - `v1.1.0` is a CLI release, it is marked Latest, and it carries no latest.json, so every installed app asking for an update gets nothing. Publishing desktop-v1.1.0 with --latest is what makes the endpoint resolve; re-probe it immediately after publishing and expect 200 with version 1.1.0. 🔴 The three existing CLI releases predate the rule and were NOT created with --latest=false; that resolves itself the moment a desktop release takes Latest, but the next CLI release must pass the flag or it will silently take Latest back and kill the updater again.

The docs site's `story/**` build exclusion is VACUOUS and must not be cited as evidence. Measured 2026-09-07 while mirroring desktop.md: `docs/story/` does not exist in the windowsweep-docs repo at all - the story artefacts live in the CLI repo - so its zero matches in `build/` prove nothing. It is a pre-emptive defence, not a tested one. The MANUAL-TASKS exclusion beside it IS genuine: that file exists in the docs repo and produces zero matches, so the entry is doing real work. Two checks that look identical in a report, one of which means something.

🔴 `docs/desktop.md` is the FIRST source page that arrives carrying its own front matter, and the docs repo now has a `.gitattributes` because of it. Every other CLI-repo page has none, and the docs site's CLAUDE.md section 4 describes front matter as something 'added on top of the mirrored body' - phrasing that assumes the source has none and says nothing about this case. The reading applied yields a byte-identical file (cmp clean, md5 300ab6ec83be1487ed13cec24f30aa39 both sides), so a re-mirror is a copy with no transformation. That is only durable because the docs repo had NO .gitattributes at all: with core.autocrlf true the mirror would have become CRLF while its source stayed LF, cmp would report a difference that is not a difference, and the natural response would be to 'fix' a file that was never wrong. Section 4 may want a sentence recording both.

🔴 BEFORE desktop-v1.2.0: latest.json's DEFAULT entry points at the MSI, and the MSI is per-machine. Measured on the published 1.1.0 manifest: `windows-x86_64` resolves to windowsweep_1.1.0_x64_en-US.msi, with `windows-x86_64-msi` and `windows-x86_64-nsis` beside it and all three signatures correctly paired. But the app INSTALLS via NSIS with installMode currentUser, and its shipped copy says the installer is per-user and needs no administrator rights - while Tauri's WiX template is perMachine with no config knob. So an in-app update would download the MSI and raise a UAC prompt, contradicting the page. It does not affect 1.1.0, because nothing updates TO it; it affects the Wave 5 proof, which is a stated success criterion (the updater verified 1.1.0 -> 1.2.0 on this machine). tauri.conf.json's plugins.updater has no `windows` block today. Decide it deliberately before 1.2.0 and test the real flow rather than the manifest.

The release workflow lost a race with GitHub's own consistency on 2026-09-07, and the diagnosis nearly went the wrong way. tauri-action created the draft, and `gh release upload` one step later failed with a bare `release not found` - which reads exactly like 'you cannot upload to a draft'. The identical command from a workstation eight minutes on succeeded against the same draft, so it is eventual consistency and the fix is a retry, not a change of mechanism. The cost of losing that race is specific and nasty: the five artefacts tauri-action attaches all arrive, the release LOOKS complete, and the one file the shipped copy promises by name - SHA256SUMS.txt - is the one missing, so the failure lands exactly where a reader would go to check the promise. The assertion step that would have caught it never ran, because the upload failed first. Now six attempts over about a minute.

RESOLVED at planning time 2026-09-07 (P4), from the plugin SOURCE rather than the manifest: the recorded risk that an in-app update would download the MSI and raise UAC does not apply to the NSIS install path. tauri-plugin-updater-2.11.0/src/updater.rs:618-624 searches [{os}-{arch}-{installer}, {os}-{arch}] in that order, and installer_for_bundle_type(bundle_type()) at :1504-1509 yields nsis for an NSIS-installed app - so the app resolves windows-x86_64-nsis and never touches the MSI entry.
